extracted.intended_audience: design patent applicants, patent practitioners, and USPTO examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Preparation and examination standards for U.S. design patent applications (drawing content, claim drafting, statutory and substantive examination criteria, and post-issuance procedures) as set out in MPEP Chapter 1500.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory subject matter for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: What kinds of designs are statutorily within patentable subject matter (includes discussion of computer-generated images, multi-article designs, and offensive content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP addresses borderline or special categories (e.g., computer-generated images, designs for multi-article assemblies, and potentially offensive designs) when determining whether the subject matter is proper for a design patent. Examiners should apply the statutory and case-law tests specific to design patents when evaluating eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a design / distinction from utility
rubrics_metrics.description: A design is the visual ornamental characteristics of an article of manufacture; it is distinct from utility patents which protect functional aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or drafting, focus on appearance/ornamentation rather than function. Functional features that are incidental to ornamentation may not be claimed as design; if the feature's existence is solely a byproduct of function and not intentionally ornamental, a lack-of-ornamentality rejection may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner representation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements governing who may represent applicants before the Office and practice in design patent matters (practitioner bar requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should ensure representation by a duly authorized/registered practitioner where required; the chapter notes practitioner-bar related requirements in the context of filing and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required application elements for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent applications consist principally of drawings, drawing descriptions, and a single claim; a brief narrative/specification is optional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the file contains the required elements: high-quality drawings (or photographs when permitted), a claim pointing to the drawing(s), and any necessary drawing descriptions. Although a prose description is optional, drawings are the heart of a design patent and must fully disclose the claimed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single claim requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent applications must contain a single claim that defines the design shown in the drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present multiple independent design claims in a single design patent application. Draft the single claim to read to the drawing(s) and include any necessary reference to broken/solid lines per drawing practice guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing specifications and visual presentation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for the content and presentation of drawings that disclose the design (use of solid vs. broken lines, clarity, completeness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solid lines define the claimed design; broken (dotted) lines show unclaimed environmental structure. Broken lines may be used to show visible environmental structure but may not be used to show hidden planes. Drawings must be clear and adequate to fully disclose the claimed ornamental features; follow MPEP detail on views, shading, and reproduction quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamentality requirement / lack of ornamentality rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Design must be ornamental — lack of ornamentality is a basis for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornamentation must have been made for the purpose of being decorative; ornament that is merely a byproduct of a functional design element may be unprotectable. Examiners may reject designs under 'lack of ornamentality' if the claimed appearance is dictated solely by function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (anticipation) for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs must be new compared to prior art designs; novelty is evaluated with regard to the visual design disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use design-appropriate novelty comparisons (visual impression tests and drawing-to-drawing comparisons). The analogous-art concept for designs is the field of actual types of design involved (i.e., designs of similar articles), not the field pertaining to the functional aspects of the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obviousness (inventive step) for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patentability requires that the claimed design not be obvious to a designer of ordinary skill (in the applicable design field) in view of the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply design-specific obviousness principles (focusing on overall visual impression and the relevant body of design prior art). Consideration of analogous art is important: compare to designs of the same or similar articles rather than functional fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112 considerations for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description/definiteness requirements as applied to design patents (i.e., the drawings and claim must comply with 35 U.S.C. 112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For designs, the drawings serve as the disclosure that must satisfy 112; the claim must point to the drawings and be definite in what is claimed. Ensure the drawings and any description together reasonably convey the claimed ornamental features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority and benefit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and requirements for claiming priority/benefit to earlier applications in design patent prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP guidance when asserting benefit/priority under relevant statutes/treaties; ensure proper referencing of earlier-filed U.S. or foreign applications and that the earlier disclosure supports the claimed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art for design analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of what constitutes analogous art in design patent examination (the relevant field is designs of the same type of article).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assembling prior art for novelty/obviousness comparisons, restrict the relevant art to designs of the same or similar articles (the actual design field), not to references merely in the same functional field of use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-issuance term and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Term of U.S. design patents: 15 years from issuance (previously 14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inform applicants of the current statutory term and any applicable calculation rules; note the change from the former 14-year term for older grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue procedures for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and processes governing the reissue of design patents (MPEP 1509).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP sets forth when and how a design patent may be reissued; follow procedural and substantive requirements for reissue applications, including timing and scope limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamination procedures for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures governing ex parte reexamination and related post-grant review processes for design patents (MPEP 1510).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the MPEP instructions for initiating and handling reexamination requests directed to design patentability issues and for the Office's processing of such proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of design patents to copyright and trademark
rubrics_metrics.description: How design patents interact with other forms of intellectual property protection (copyright, trademark).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP discusses overlap and differences (scope, subject matter, remedies, and enforcement) between design patents and copyright/trademark protection; applicants should consider parallel filings and enforcement strategies where appropriate.
